title: Lorenzo de Medici Sails to Naples
text:
In April 1478 conspirators backed by the Pazzi family and supported by Pope Sixtus IV attacked Lorenzo de Medici and his brother Giuliano during Mass in Florence cathedral. Giuliano was killed; Lorenzo escaped wounded. Florence executed the conspirators, including an archbishop, and the pope responded by excommunicating Lorenzo and placing the city under interdict. With King Ferrante of Naples as his ally, Sixtus made war on Florence.

The war went badly for Florence. Its troops were beaten, its territory raided, and its own allies were unreliable. By late 1479 the city was exhausted, and some Florentines were beginning to blame Lorenzo, since the enemies said they fought him, not the city.

In December 1479 Lorenzo made an extraordinary decision. Without a guarantee of safety, he sailed from Pisa to Naples to put himself in the hands of the enemy king. The risk was real: Ferrante had a reputation for treachery and had once had a visiting commander arrested and killed despite a safe conduct. Lorenzo wrote to the Florentine government that, since he was the one the enemy wanted, he would go himself.

Lorenzo spent about three months at Ferrante's court. He argued that a strong Florence was a better friend to Naples than an ambitious papacy, and he charmed the court. In March 1480 a peace was agreed. Lorenzo returned to Florence to great acclaim, his position stronger than ever.
lesson: Sometimes the direct, personal approach to an adversary can achieve what force cannot. Understand what he really wants and show him that his interests lie with you.
people: Lorenzo de Medici, Ferrante of Naples, Pope Sixtus IV
source: Lorenzo de Medici's letter to the Signoria of Florence (December 1479); Niccolo Machiavelli, Florentine Histories, book 8
